A Skulk that wanders too far from the ol:
A Skulk that wanders too far from the old roads usually dies of it. The ones that went east into the ash barrens after the Sundering did not, quite. The ground there was still warm, and they learned to lie in it, and after enough generations of lying in the ground the ground began to lie in them. A Cinder Skulk is leaner than its cousins, black as a spent coal, with seams of orange under the scales that brighten when it breathes in.

It has also lost the family patience. A road Skulk waits at the narrowing for the last one in line. A Cinder Skulk does not wait for anything. It crosses the field in one low leap, comes down on whoever is standing furthest back hard enough to stagger everyone near them, and bites.

The bite is what the barrens added. The jaws run hot enough to seal the wound they make, and the seal goes on burning after the teeth let go. It is the only wound the surgeons of the eastern towns treat by cooling first.
A Volthex has no parent and no childhood:
A Volthex has no parent and no childhood. Where raw mana pools in a low place and sits long enough, it begins to order itself — first into crusts, then into lattices, then into something that turns to face you. Nobody has satisfactorily explained the last step. The scholars who study them are careful to say *grown* rather than *born*, and careful not to say *thinks*.

In a fight a Volthex works like the light it is made of. It scatters first, throwing razor shards in glittering volleys that seem almost decorative until the third one opens a throat, and this is not random — it is thinning, the way you thin a crowd before you need a clear line. Then every facet turns inward at once, the whole body dimming as the light is gathered, and a single prism-beam goes through plate armour as though the armour had been a suggestion.

They cannot be reasoned with, bribed, or frightened. They can be shattered, and that is the entire tactical literature on the subject.
A Whisp remembers being alive and has ne:
A Whisp remembers being alive and has never forgiven the arrangement. It is a small flame, patient, and it burns at roughly the brightness of a lamp carried by someone about a hundred paces ahead of you on a dark road — which is not an accident and is the entire strategy.

Follow it and it lights you: a clinging fire that will not be smothered or beaten out, that goes where you go. Then it drops guttering embers behind itself, and the embers take, and the patch of ground behind you becomes as impassable as the dark in front. A Whisp does not need to be strong. It only needs you to keep choosing the light.

Hedge-wisdom in the border villages is very old and very short on this point: *if the lamp ahead never gets closer, it is not a lamp.* Every generation there are people who work this out too late, and every generation the Whisps are a little further down the road.
A marsh can be poisoned for a long time:
A marsh can be poisoned for a long time before anything comes of it. Then the rot reaches some threshold, and what crawls out is Bilewretch — armour-plated across the skull, endlessly oozing everywhere else, moving with the unbothered slowness of a thing that has never in its life needed to hurry.

It hawks globs of hissing acid that keep eating long after they land, so a company fighting one is always fighting the last thirty seconds as well as the current ones. Press in close to end it quickly and it swells and ruptures, flinging a wave of clinging slime that leaves everyone caught in it burning and bogged down and precisely as slow as Bilewretch is.

That is the whole design, if a marsh can be said to design. You do not out-trade a Bilewretch. You either kill it from range at enormous expense, or you close, and it makes you into something that moves at its speed, and then the pace of the fight is entirely its own.
A midden is not dangerous. Twenty midden:
A midden is not dangerous. Twenty middens layered over four hundred years, in a city that never once carted its refuse beyond the walls, eventually is. Sludgemaw is what rot becomes when enough of it accumulates in one place and begins, slowly, to want.

It dresses itself. That is the detail that unsettles people who have only heard about them: a Sludgemaw scavenges plate from whatever it has previously eaten and works it into its own bulk until blows land with a dull sound and barely mark it. Beneath the salvaged armour there is no body to speak of, only a maw of broken teeth — cutlery, blade-fragments, the jawbones of earlier meals — and a lunge that is far quicker than the shambling gait suggests.

Every bite mends it. This is the whole problem with Sludgemaw. A prolonged fight against one is a fight in which your side is being converted, piece by piece, into the reason you are losing.
Blackquill was an ordinary bird for the:
Blackquill was an ordinary bird for the first part of a very long life. Battlefields changed that. Something in the Emberweave rewards a scavenger that keeps returning to the same kind of ground, and Blackquill returned to it for three centuries and grew fat, then large, then clever, and then something for which *bird* is a courtesy.

It opens by lashing the front line with a storm of razor feathers — a shrieking, blinding thing that does less damage than it appears to and is not meant to do damage at all. It is meant to make a company look up. The murder comes down while they are looking, an unkindness of black shapes falling on the whole formation at once from an angle nobody was watching.

Soldiers who have survived it describe the same detail unprompted: that the bird itself did not join in, and stayed above, and seemed to be counting.
Calling a Vexmite *it* is a convenience. A Vexmite is a seething knot of stingers and wings that moves and reacts as one spiteful animal, and if you divide the cloud in half you have two smaller Vexmites and a worse afternoon. Where the cohesion comes from is not known. It survives being scattered, drowned, and set on fire.

It picks one target and falls on them in a blur, and the individual stings barely register — a prickling, a heat, an itch. That is by design, insofar as anything about a Vexmite is. Each sting leaves a fraction of venom, and the arithmetic does the rest, so that a soldier who walked away irritated is on the ground an hour later while the cloud is four valleys distant and entirely uninterested.

Field medics rank Vexmite wounds as low-priority on sight and have lost more patients to that judgement than to any monster in the bestiary.
Chimney sweeps have a word for the thing:
Chimney sweeps have a word for the thing that lives at the top of a flue nobody has swept in a hundred years. The sweeps who have seen one tend to find other work.

A Sootwing Imp is what a century of soot becomes when it settles thickly enough to hold a shape. It is small, horned and grinning, with ragged wings and eyes like two freshly blown coals, and it is noticeably less solid below the waist than above; its lower half trails away into smoke that never finishes rising. The lantern it carries on a crooked stick is its one treasure. An imp will abandon a fight to recover it.

It prefers to stay out of reach and throw. A flick of the stick sends a needle of ember across the field, thin and very hot. When something gets close, the imp simply comes apart. The whole creature billows into a cloud of soot, most of what strikes it passes through the way a hand passes through smoke, and when the cloud clears it is still there, still grinning, still holding the lantern.
Crows gather at dusk. Anyone who has liv:
Crows gather at dusk. Anyone who has lived near a rookery knows the hour: the sky goes black with them, the noise is enormous, and then, all at once, they fall silent. The old word for that hour is vespers. The name for what came down out of the rookery at Rookhallow Abbey is Sable Vesper.

It stands like a tall cantor in a black choir robe stitched with tarnished gold, with a crow's long beak for a face. The robe is not cloth. It is crows, hundreds of them, pressed wing to wing. It raises a tuning fork of dark iron, and when it strikes the note, they sing.

What they sing is a dirge, and it is not for the enemy. It mends its own side, swelling each time it is sung, a healing hymn that sounds like a funeral. For the enemy there is something plainer: five crows peel from the hem and go out as black darts, each to a different throat among the nearest. And every few breaths, one enemy somewhere on the field finds their voice taken for a moment by the hour when the crows go quiet. The bell at Rookhallow has not been rung by a human hand in a century. It rings every evening regardless.
Every Ashen was a pyromancer who found t:
Every Ashen was a pyromancer who found the ceiling of their talent and went through it anyway. The fire that kills a fire-mage does not always let go. What walks afterward is the skeleton and the habit — no memory, no name, no particular malice, just the muscle-knowledge of a discipline practised so long that the bones kept it after everything else burned away.

They fight like teachers. A pointed finger, and a foe is alight; a sweep of the arm, and a rain of embers falls in a wide arc, laying down a smouldering patch that eats anyone who stands in it. These are first-year forms. An Ashen performs them with the terrible clean precision of someone who has done the exercise ten thousand times and no longer needs to think.

Temples that once trained pyromancers now keep a standing bounty on them, quietly, and do not discuss why the descriptions in the bounty notices are so specific about the posture.
Every Mimic is a lie about treasure. The:
Every Mimic is a lie about treasure. The Nightcap is the version that got lazy: a Mimic that sat too long in one damp cellar waiting for a fool, until the rot got into the lid and something grew out of it, a broad violet mushroom cap, glossy and speckled, with a sweet smell like bread left to rise.

The rot went all the way down. It walks now on legs of root and fungus, and the chest has gone soft at the corners. By any sensible measure it is dying. It has not noticed, and it has discovered that the mushroom is a better lure than gold ever was, because people who would never open a strange chest will happily stoop to pick a strange mushroom.

Then the lid comes down. The bite leaves its victim dazed, bleeding and unable to pull free. When there are too many of them, the cap shivers and a violet cloud of spores drifts over the crowd, and everyone breathing it turns heavy-limbed and very slow, and begins, gently, to be digested. Cellar-keepers in the old cities check their mushrooms before their locks.
Every foundry town in the Iron Reach had:
Every foundry town in the Iron Reach had a slag heap, and every slag heap had Furnace Gnawers, which is roughly how the foundrymen knew the heap was still warm. They began as scavengers, drawn to the dribbles of hot metal the pourers spilled, and after enough generations of eating it they lost the ability to eat anything else. The inside of a Gnawer's mouth glows. That is not a figure of speech. At night you can see a pack coming by its teeth.

When the foundries went cold, one by one, the Gnawers went looking for heat elsewhere, and found that people are warm.

They fight like the scavengers they are. A quick snap at whoever is nearest, and the bite leaves a scorch that keeps smouldering under the skin. Then a sideways scramble through the ash, claws digging, and a spray of loose coals kicked into the faces of everyone in front, still burning when it lands. Old foundrymen leave a cooling ingot at the end of the heap on the last night of the year. None of them will say what it is for.
Every labyrinth needs something at its c:
Every labyrinth needs something at its centre, or it is only a garden with ambitions. The glassmakers of Tellary built theirs from mirror and crystal as a monument to their craft, and put a bull in it as a joke. The bull did not find it funny. It spent eleven years learning the maze wall by wall, and somewhere in those years the walls began to learn it back.

Orryx came out of the labyrinth larger than any bull has a right to be and standing on two legs, clad in black plate grown through with violet crystal. The plan of the maze is traced across his chest in lines of blue light, and it changes as he breathes. His axe has a head of solid crystal that nobody gave him.

Nothing moves him. He was built by walls, and he fights like one. Hooks and chains slide off him, and blows meant to throw him back simply stop. When he charges, it is at the farthest enemy, straight down a path only he can see, and the ground shakes where he lands. When he swings the axe, its edge sheds splinters that fly into the nearest foes like thrown glass. Tellary sealed the labyrinth after he left. There was no point. He is carrying it.
Every navy keeps a list of its admirals,:
Every navy keeps a list of its admirals, and on the old fleet rolls of the western ports there is one line with the name scraped out. The rank is there. The dates are there. His ships are listed, all eleven, and beside each the same note: lost with all hands. The name was struck by order of the admiralty.

He is still sailing. The Nameless Admiral walks out of sea-fog in a captain's long coat and a tricorn gone green with age, soaked through and glowing faintly blue at the seams. He carries an anchor the way other officers carry a sword, and it drips.

His crews are the ones he lost, and he commands them still. When he lifts his hand, the ghost of a broadside answers: one roaring shot of pale, shrieking souls fired down the enemy line, tearing through everyone in its path to the far end. When he chooses a man, he throws the anchor. It takes hold of the farthest enemy he can see and drags them back across the field to his feet, helpless as a ship on a lee shore. Nobody living knows his name. The drowned know it. He has never once let one of them go.
Every sailor who drowns belongs to someo:
Every sailor who drowns belongs to someone. That is the first law of the Drowned Court, and Nerissa is the one they belong to. She was a queen above the water once, of a harbour kingdom whose name has worn off every map, and she took her flagship into a storm she had been warned about because her fleet was watching. The fleet followed her down. She calls that loyalty. The widows called it something else.

On the bottom she found that a crown does not stop working just because the head beneath it has stopped breathing. She holds court in the wreck of her flagship, under a crown of white coral that grows a tine for every ship lost off her old coast. Her gown is water.

She fights like a monarch passing judgement. At a gesture the tide sweeps a whole wing of the enemy off its feet. The pearl on her sceptre is her sentence; it falls on one chosen enemy like a dropped anchor and leaves them senseless. And she does not tire. The sea pays her a tithe, a little strength returned with every pull of the tide, so the longer the fight runs, the more she has in hand. She has never lost a subject. She is always gaining them.
Forty years he kept them and they never:
Forty years he kept them and they never once had to think about it. The grass was where he said the grass was; the danger was whatever he put himself between. Then an army came through the valley on its way somewhere else, and the herd was in the road, and that was the whole of it.

What comes up out of the floor now is not quite what went into it. They are bigger, and they are armoured in plate nobody remembers forging, and each of them carries a short sword and a round shield they were certainly never buried with. They do not speak. They form a line in front of Hurne without being told, every time, in the same order — the way animals that have shared a field for a long time know exactly where they stand relative to one another.

They will hold that line until it kills them, and then he will call, and they will come up again.
Frostjaw Trolls live above the snowline:
Frostjaw Trolls live above the snowline because nothing up there is warm enough to argue with them. They are enormous, blue as a drowned man and furred with rime, with beards of icicles that clack when they chew. Trolls regrow what they lose, as everyone knows. A Frostjaw regrows it in ice, so that an old one is half glacier, and creaks.

They hang skulls from their belts, not all of them from animals. This is not cruelty. A Frostjaw keeps skulls because it keeps everything; the caves they sleep in are packed to the ceiling with things carried up the mountain for no reason anyone has worked out.

They carry ice the same way, and fight with it. A Frostjaw heaves a block of glacier over its head and throws it, and it bursts where it lands into a spray of freezing shards. When anything gets close it lifts one foot and brings it down, and the cold goes out through the ground in a ring and locks everyone caught in it where they stand. Then it picks them up and considers whether to keep them.
Gnashul is what happens when hunger outl:
Gnashul is what happens when hunger outlasts the body that had it. The claws are the least of it — they leave wounds that will not close, ragged things that go on bleeding hours after the fight, which is unpleasant but survivable with a competent surgeon and enough thread.

It is the bite that ends people. Gnashul's bite rots the *magic* meant to mend it. A healer laying hands on the wound feels the working go in and simply drain away, and the more they pour in the less comes back, until they are spending themselves for nothing on a soldier who is dying at exactly the rate they cannot slow. The longer Gnashul stays attached to someone, the less any healer can do.

Companies that fight ghoul fiends regularly adopt an ugly doctrine: kill the Gnashul before treating anyone it has bitten. It is correct, and it is not a thing anyone volunteers to explain to the wounded.
Granith was made to dig, and it outlived:
Granith was made to dig, and it outlived the company that made it by a hundred and forty years. Nobody switched it off, because switching it off was a task on somebody's list and the somebody died. It kept the shafts clear for a while after that. Then the shafts collapsed, and it kept the tools.

It heaves broken rubble across a field with the indifference of a machine moving spoil, and this is survivable. What is not survivable is the pickaxe. Granith has held on to it through everything — worn to a shine at the haft, the head chipped and rehardened by a century of striking stone — and when a fight has run long enough Granith throws it, unerringly, at whoever is standing farthest back. It goes through everyone in the line on the way.

Mining charters in the region still carry a clause about recovering company property. The clause is older than the Emberweave, and no one has ever tried to enforce it.
Gravediggers in the hill parishes work i:
Gravediggers in the hill parishes work in pairs, by a rule older than anyone can explain: one digs, one watches the neighbouring plots. The Graveclaw Ghoul is the explanation. It comes up from underneath, having dug the whole way from the last churchyard it emptied, and its claws are the proof: long, hooked, scoured bright by the earth and worn to an edge that would shame a sickle.

It is hunched and wiry and armoured in scraps of whatever it has dug through, black leather and planks of somebody's coffin lid. Something burns a sickly green in its ribs where a heart ought to be.

The claws come in threes, across and back and across again, and each pass opens the last one wider. When the ghoul is hurt it does the thing that made the parishes write their rule down. It stops fighting for a moment and feeds, and what it tears out of its enemy goes straight into mending itself. A ghoul that has eaten well is a ghoul that will not die tonight.
Graveyard roses grow, as everyone knows,:
Graveyard roses grow, as everyone knows, extremely well. The gardeners of the old cemetery at Carrowell stopped asking why theirs grew quite so well the year the lower terraces began to sink, and stopped asking anything at all the year the terraces slid into the river.

What came up out of that ground is the Rotbloom Ooze: a low, heaving mound of green-black slime with the roses still growing out of it, dark and full-blown and smelling of funerals. Things float in it, mostly skulls. Whether the Ooze ate them or simply came up with them does not seem to matter to the Ooze.

It fights with what it came from. A glob of green acid spat at whoever is closest goes on eating long after it lands. Worse is the flood. The Ooze surges up and breaks over one enemy in a wave of grave water, and afterwards no wound of theirs will close; healers pour everything they have into them and watch it run off like rain from a slate. The roses, the gardeners will tell you, are very beautiful. Nobody at Carrowell plants them any more.
Grommash is a mountain of muscle and sca:
Grommash is a mountain of muscle and scar tissue that has never once been made to kneel, and the list of things that have tried is long, well-attested, and includes two gods.

Its club turns armour to paste. Its warbellow scatters the brave — not the cowardly, who have usually already gone; the brave, who were standing their ground when the sound arrived and who afterward cannot explain what happened to them. And nothing holds it. No chain, no binding spell, no frost, no root, no working of any school has ever kept Grommash in a place it had decided to leave. Scholars have made careers out of the question. The prevailing answer is unsatisfying: it is not that Grommash resists these things. It is that they appear to be applied to something that is not quite where Grommash is.

It comes when it wants. It leaves when it wants. In six hundred years of records there is no instance of anything at all altering either decision.
Grundle plants itself where the line nee:
Grundle plants itself where the line needs to hold and dares the world to move it. It was built for exactly this and nothing else — no reach, no speed, no cleverness, just an enormous tolerance for being hit and a stomp that sends a slowing tremor out through the ground and turns a charge into a wade.

The danger is not Grundle. Everyone understands this and nobody manages to act on it. A Grundle occupies attention the way a fire in the room occupies attention: every eye and every blade drifts toward it, and while they drift, whatever is standing behind it works unmolested. Commanders shout themselves hoarse ordering their people past it. Their people go around it and then, without deciding to, come back.

The makers are long gone. What survives of their doctrine is a single line, recovered from a foundry wall: *the wall is not the weapon.*
Grushak is not a leader of a warband. Gr:
Grushak is not a leader of a warband. Grushak is a warband, in the sense that engaging him requires the same number of people, the same preparation, and produces the same casualties. He came south during the third migration and simply never left, and the settlements that were there when he arrived are marked on current maps as terrain features.

He fights like a landslide, which is to say without any interest in your formation. One swing goes through a whole cluster because he does not distinguish between the man he is aiming at and the two standing near him. When a line holds, he stomps, and the ground buckles, and everyone on it goes down together — after which the swinging resumes on people who are already lying on their backs.

Three separate armies have claimed to have killed him. All three claims are considered plausible. None of them has stopped him being reported again the following spring.
Herders on the slopes below the fire mou:
Herders on the slopes below the fire mountains call them Ashfang, and will tell you that nobody has ever seen one alone. A Magma Hound is a lean wolf of black stone that never finished setting. When it runs, the cracks along its back open and the fire underneath streams out through its mane and trails from its paws, so that a pack crossing a hillside at night leaves a burning line that takes hours to go out.

They hunt like wolves, which is to say by choosing. Not the strongest and not the nearest, but whoever stands furthest back and feels safest. The hound crosses the whole field for that one in a single streak of fire and hits the ground beside them hard enough to leave the whole cluster reeling.

Then it howls. The herders call it a summons, but the howl is mostly for the hound itself. It is working itself up, and for the next few seconds it bites and tears far faster than any wolf should. A whole pack howling together is a sound the slopes have learned to empty out for.
In the Bright Waste the mirages come at:
In the Bright Waste the mirages come at noon, and this one comes when Zahri Sunhorn calls it. It begins as a point of pale gold hanging in the air beside her, no bigger than a seed, and then the heat catches it and it opens all at once into a shape: horned, long-haired, lance in hand, hooves planted in the sand. It is her, blurred at the edges the way the horizon blurs at midday, and lit from within by a light that does not match the sun.

It has none of her tricks. It cannot find the gap in an enemy's armour or run a line to its far end. It has a third of her strength and a single purpose, to stand at her side and put its lance into whatever she is fighting, and it holds to that until something breaks it apart. Only then does she call another.

Zahri calls it the herd. She knows better, and says so; it is only her, thinner. But it runs at her shoulder the way they used to, and it has never once turned toward the water.
In the Sunkfen the islands move. Not qui:
In the Sunkfen the islands move. Not quickly and not far, but the fen-cutters stopped charting the smaller hummocks long ago, because a hummock that sat east of the old weir in spring is often west of it by autumn, and in a bad year it is gone.

Many of those hummocks are Mudsnap Crabs. They bury themselves in the silt when young and do not surface for decades, and by then there is a small drowned-looking tree growing out of the shell, roots down through the plates, moss on the rim, and a heron's nest if the crab is unlucky. Travellers step onto them. Travellers are rarely surprised for long.

A green claw comes out from under the moss, closes on whoever is nearest and hauls them in against the shell, and holds them while they struggle. Then the crab heaves, and the mud around it bursts up in a sour grey-green spray that clings to everyone near, dragging at every step and eating at whatever it touches. Fen-cutters test each new hummock with a pole before they land. It is the first thing their children are taught.
In the third winter of the Rift the sky:
In the third winter of the Rift the sky over the northern valleys cracked, and for a season you could see through the cracks into somewhere else. The cracks closed. Some of what had been living in them did not go back.

A Riftling Spider is the size of a hunting dog, grown from violet crystal rather than chitin, faceted and jagged, on legs that end in long glassy spikes. It does not entirely agree with the place it is standing in; watch one long enough and its edges seem to be in two places at once. It spins its web from the same crystal, invisible until it catches the light, and throws it rather than hanging it.

The web lands on one target and holds them completely, pinned between one moment and the next. That is the spider's patience. Its hunger comes after. It stops being where it was and starts being behind the weakest thing on the field, and bites, and the bite goes deep. Survivors all say the same thing: the spider never crossed the distance. It simply declined to be anywhere in between.
In the western hills there is a hall of:
In the western hills there is a hall of mirrors built by a king who could not bear to be alone and could not bear anyone else. Every surface in it was polished silver, so that he was never without company. When he died the hall was sealed with him inside, and the reflections were left with nothing to reflect.

One of them walked out. Asterion is tall and thin and made entirely of mirror, plated in silver too bright to look at, cloaked in violet, and circled by long silver shards like a looking-glass that has not finished falling. It has no face of its own. It wears whatever face is looking at it.

Every few moments a blow meant for Asterion lands on a reflection instead, and the reflection shatters, and the warden is standing a pace to one side, unmarked. Every wound it deals mends it a little. When pressed, the shards close around it like a shield wall and turn most of what strikes them. And it catches the light and throws it back, a lance of brilliance that goes straight through the enemy line to the last one standing. It is searching the hills for the king. It has not understood that it is what remains of him.
It is a wolf, and that is not an acciden:
It is a wolf, and that is not an accident. Of all the small entries in the Librarian's book, the one he reaches for first is the grey wolf of the lowland farms: three pages near the front, in a careful younger hand. He wrote it the winter after Brisk, sitting in the snow by a sheepfold until he had it right, so that he would never again need anything larger for wolves.

Torn out and folded into a seal, the page lands on the field and opens into what it describes: a lean, low wolf of wet black ink with violet light in its eyes, its edges forever curling off into spatters as though it were still being written. It does exactly what a wolf does and nothing more. It picks a quarry, runs it down, and bites until the quarry stops. It has no tricks. He did not write it any.

When the chapter ends it runs back into the page, and the page goes back in the book. He never sends more than three. Three, he has found, is enough for nearly anything a wolf is for.
Leviath is the drowned deep given shape:
Leviath is the drowned deep given shape and spite — not a creature of the sea so much as an argument the sea has been having with the shore, made large enough to walk.

It rolls a wall of water across the front rank and erupts geysers beneath the ones who thought they had found a gap, and for the opening minutes it is a hard fight rather than an impossible one. That is the trap, and it has taken better companies than yours. The longer Leviath is left standing, the more the ocean's fury builds behind every blow — not faster, not cleverer, simply *heavier* — until a fight that was being won is one that cannot be survived, and the change happens somewhere nobody can point to afterward.

Every account of a successful hunt describes the same thing: a decision, early, that felt like panic at the time. Every account of a failure describes a company that was doing well and saw no reason to change what was working.
Lost Souls are the lanterns of people wh:
Lost Souls are the lanterns of people who died somewhere nobody came back for. Drowned crews, sealed miners, the garrisons of forts that were relieved a week too late. They drift in the place it happened and they do not remember it — grief is all that survived the crossing, and grief without its story is just a light in the dark going slowly nowhere.

They fling bolts of cold soul-light, which is the closest thing they have to speech. It is when one draws close that the trouble starts. A Lost Soul does not attack so much as *enter*, and the hero it finds is abruptly holding somebody else's last ten minutes — the water coming up, the roof coming down, the certainty that the relief column is on its way. They stand frozen through all of it. From outside it lasts a moment.

Priests will tell you the kindest thing is to end them. Priests are also the ones who ask, afterward, whether anyone caught a name.
Lost Souls drift where they died and rem:
Lost Souls drift where they died and remember nothing. A Wispweaver Shade is what happens when one of them remembers a single thing and will not let it go, and the thing is almost always a voice: someone who called for it, or someone it called for, at the end, in the dark.

The Shade is a tall hooded tatter of violet shadow carrying a small lantern, and its fingers trail threads of pale light that it knots and unknots without pause, like someone working at a problem in their sleep. The threads are voices. Nobody has proven this. Everyone who has been caught in one believes it.

A single thread flicks out, wraps a throat and pulls tight, and whoever is on the end of it cannot move or cast or cry out until it lets go. Then the lantern gutters and the Shade is simply elsewhere. It comes out of the shadow behind the weakest person on the field and takes hold of them with both cold hands. It is listening, always, for the voice it lost. It has never yet been the right one.
Magmourn burns from the inside out — a f:
Magmourn burns from the inside out — a furnace that was given a mind and was given nothing else, no body worth the name, no purpose, no way to put itself out. Whether that was punishment or an accident depends on which fragment of the record you trust, and both fragments were written by people with reasons to lie.

It hurls fireballs that burst like small falling suns, and when cornered it stops aiming and sets the entire field alight at once, which is less a tactic than an admission. The real danger is simply proximity: the air around Magmourn is hot enough to be its own slow death, and companies have lost their rear ranks to a monster none of them ever came within forty paces of.

It does not pursue. It has never been observed to pursue anything. It goes where it is going, and it is always going somewhere, and the maps of where it has been are kept by an order whose entire purpose is making sure the line does not intersect a settlement twice.
Mordath was a knight, and by the account:
Mordath was a knight, and by the accounts that survive, a good one. What is also recorded is the bargain: at the end, offered the choice between dying well and continuing, he chose to continue, and the thing that offered him the choice was scrupulous about honouring the letter of it.

He continues. The bone-winged husk wades into the front rank and carves everything in front of it in a single reaping arc, and with every wound it opens a thread of stolen life crawls back up the soul-forged blade into the hollow where a heart used to beat. The longer the melee runs, the stronger he gets, feeding on the very ranks he is cutting down.

The cruelty of the bargain is in the wording. He was granted the ability to keep swinging, and nothing else — not rest, not an ending, not the capacity to decide he has had enough. Somewhere under the helm is a man who has been fighting continuously for six hundred years and cannot stop of his own accord, and everyone who faces him is, in a sense he can no longer articulate, doing him a favour they will not survive.
Most dryads are rooted, and die with the:
Most dryads are rooted, and die with their tree. The Skyroot is the exception. On the high cliffs of the eastern coast the trees grow with their roots half in the air, clinging to bare rock, and now and then a gale tears one loose. Most fall. A few, it seems, decided not to.

A Skyroot Dryad is tall and thin and made of pale twisting wood, with leaves the blue of distance and roots that trail beneath her like a torn hem, never quite touching the ground. Butterflies follow her everywhere for the sap, and she lets them.

She does not like to fight and is good at it anyway. A branch that looked like an arm cracks out as a whip of briar and lays open whatever it touches. When her side is hurting she opens the bark along her arms and lets the sap run, and the sweet scent of it drifts over all her allies and their wounds begin to close. She is the only tree from her cliff that got up after the gale. She has been making up for it ever since.
Nightgloom throws bolts of pure absence:
Nightgloom throws bolts of pure absence — not darkness, which is only the lack of light, but a hole in the place where a thing was, that closes afterward slightly wrong. Anyone struck describes the same sensation: not pain, but a brief and total conviction that they have forgotten something they cannot afford to have forgotten.

Cornered, it stops throwing and simply exhales. The dark comes out in a soft spreading pulse, and it finds everyone — behind cover, behind a shield wall, behind the assumption that being at the back of the formation is the same as being safe. There is no line of sight to break, because Nightgloom is not looking.

It appears where light has recently and violently failed: burned-out watchfires, cities that went dark in one night, the lower levels of the vaults. Whether it causes the failure or arrives afterward is an open argument, and the people best placed to settle it were present for the failure.
On the high meadows above the Shardwood:
On the high meadows above the Shardwood the grass grows glassy, and the herds that graze there grow glassier. A Crystalhorn Grazer begins life as something close to an ordinary mountain deer. Every season it eats the crystal-laced grass, and every season the crystal comes out through the hide: first a crust along the spine, then shards, then a whole mantle of pale blue prisms that chime as it walks. The old stags look like chandeliers. They sound like them too.

They are herd animals, and nervous ones, and dangerous out of all proportion to their temper. A startled Grazer shivers, and its outer shards break loose and fly, three at a time, into whoever is nearest. It regrows them within a day.

When it decides to run, it runs at the problem. It crosses the field head down for whoever stands farthest off and hits the ground beside them in a burst of cold light and splintering crystal that leaves everyone near stunned. Hunters prize the horns. The herds have learned what hunters look like, and on the high meadows these days it is the hunters who are nervous.
Ooznik does not fight. Fighting implies:
Ooznik does not fight. Fighting implies an opponent. Ooznik digests, and everything in front of it is at some stage of that process.

It opens by spraying a searing acid across the front rank, which is efficient rather than cruel — armour is simply the first course. Wound it and you will not find that useful either: an Ooznik under pressure divides, folds a piece of itself away, and reincorporates it a moment later with the damage no longer present. There is no organ to strike, no centre to break, and no observable point at which it decides it has had enough.

The only reliable method is heat, applied continuously, faster than it can shed the damaged portion. This is well documented. It is also expensive, slow, and requires standing close to an Ooznik for a sustained period, which is why the well-documented method is so rarely the one anybody uses.
Rustclank hums. That is how you know it:
Rustclank hums. That is how you know it is close before you see it — a low electrical note in the fillings and the buckles, scavenged current running through a frame that was assembled out of at least four other machines by something with no understanding of any of them.

It opens by yanking the nearest fighter off their feet with a magnetic pull, straight into the grinding gearwork of its chest, which does to armour what armour is not designed to survive. Then it overclocks — gears spinning past every tolerance they were built for, blows landing faster and faster, the whole thing shrieking as it goes — until either the target gives way or Rustclank does.

It usually does. That is not comfort. A Rustclank tearing itself apart at full speed is still striking twice a second, and it has never once been observed to slow down in order to survive.
She led the herd before Hurne did, in th:
She led the herd before Hurne did, in the sense that mattered: the others watched her, and where she settled the rest settled. He would tell you she ran the valley and he only carried the water.

Whatever she is now, it kept that. She comes up out of the ground last, always, after the others are already standing, and the first thing she does is walk the line and put the sick ones right. The chant is not a language anyone has identified and the bone-staff was not made by hands; the effect is simply that wounds close near her, and that anyone who crowds her herd begins, without being touched, to burn.

Hurne does not give her orders. It has been observed, more than once, that when the two of them are on a field together it is not entirely clear which one is being followed.
Shellwark is two animals depending on th:
Shellwark is two animals depending on the minute. For most of a fight it is barely an animal at all — tucked in, plates locked, an object that weapons happen to. Attacking it during this phase is not dangerous. It is simply pointless, and Shellwark can wait longer than a company can swing.

Then it comes out spinning. The shell that was a wall becomes a fortress in motion, edged plate carving in a wide circle, and everyone who spent the last minute closing to hit something that would not break is now standing exactly where they should not be. It does not chase. It does not need to. It has already been given the position it wanted by people who came to it.

Old campaigners give the same advice and are ignored for the same reason every time: back off and let it open. Nobody likes standing in a field doing nothing while a monster ignores them.
Ships' cats go overboard more often than:
Ships' cats go overboard more often than sailors do, and most of them drown. The Reef Prowler is what the southern reefs made of the few that did not. It still has a cat's lines, a cat's whiskers and a cat's opinion of everyone, but the fur has become scales that shift from blue to rose in the light, the ears have become fins, and the tail ends in a fluke, which it uses exactly as a cat uses its tail: to express contempt.

It hunts tide pools, and treats a battlefield as one. It waits until the line has settled, then goes straight through the front of it in one long lunge and lands among the ones at the very back, raking as it comes down. Nobody expects a cat to start at the far end.

Its other trick is the one sailors fear. It hooks its claws into whoever is farthest from it and pulls, the way an undertow pulls, and they are dragged helpless across the field and dropped at its feet. The scholars say it works the current. The sailors say it simply wants them more.
Skarrn are bred, not born. Deep beneath:
Skarrn are bred, not born. Deep beneath the Shardwood the hives hang in resonant galleries where the rock itself rings at a single unchanging note, and the drones are grown inside that note until their wings answer it. A Skarrn does not tire the way living things tire. It winds up. The first exchange is almost sluggish; by the fourth its wings have found the hive-note and it is striking faster than the eye follows, and the crystal stinger takes a sip of something vital back with every hit.

That is the part the survivors describe wrongly. They say it got faster because it smelled blood. It did not. It got faster because nothing had yet made it stop, and a Skarrn left alone simply continues accelerating until the fight ends or it does. Veteran companies kill the drone that looks least dangerous first, on the understanding that in ninety seconds it will be the only one that matters. Those who do not learn this lose whole squads to a single insect that was, at the opening of the engagement, the slowest thing on the field.
Skulk are patient in a way that reads as:
Skulk are patient in a way that reads as intelligence and probably is not. They live in the rubble of the collapsed roads — the old imperial routes that dropped into their own foundations during the Sundering — and they do not hunt so much as wait beside the places where a path narrows and a column has to string out single file.

They take the last one. Always the last one. A long stone-knuckled arm comes out of the dark and whatever it closes on is gone before the sound of it reaches the head of the line, and by the time anyone turns there is only a slightly disturbed patch of gravel and a gap in the marching order. What the Skulk does next is unhurried, because it has already won: one heavy blow to leave its catch dazed and unable to call out, and then the long drag back into the stone.

Caravan masters count heads at every narrowing. It is not superstition. It is the only defence that has ever worked.
Storm Eels hatch in the sky. Their mothe:
Storm Eels hatch in the sky. Their mother lays them inside the thunderheads, each egg a ball of lightning the size of a man's head, and the hatchling coils around its own yolk and carries it for the rest of its life. That is the crackling sphere a Storm Eel never lets go of. It is also, the scholars suspect, the only thing keeping it alive outside the cloud.

They swim through open air as if it were deep water, all ridged spine and ragged blue fin, leaving the smell of rain behind them. A Storm Eel prefers not to touch anything. It lets the charge go in three forked lashes, each finding a different body among whoever is closest.

When it has gathered enough, it does touch. The eel winds itself up like a spring and lets go, crossing the whole field in an instant to strike the farthest enemy in a burst of water and lightning that leaves everyone near them twitching. Then it hangs in the air, crackling, and begins to wind up again. Fishermen who see one turn for home.
Storm Eels have a mother. Nobody believe:
Storm Eels have a mother. Nobody believed it until an expedition from Highcombe climbed into the thunderheads to find where the eels came from, and the two who came back had gone white-haired and would say only that the nest was the size of a town, and that she had been sitting on it.

Maelvara is a woman to the waist and a bird of prey below, with talons that could close around a horse and wings so wide and dark that she is less a creature in flight than weather on the move. Lightning crawls through her feathers, and her crest sparks at the tips. The Stormnest is woven from lightning-struck timber and the ribs of ships, and every clutch she lays hatches into eels that coil away through the sky to hunt.

She leaves the nest only when something threatens it, and she is not gentle. She drops out of the cloud onto the nearest enemy and strikes three times with her talons, each blow landing like a thunderclap. Then she spreads her wings and sings, and the air begins to turn, and a choir of whirling wind descends on the enemy, grinding them and slowing them while her children close in. She has lost eggs before. Highcombe has never been forgiven for it.
Sylphice coils through the tide like a l:
Sylphice coils through the tide like a living current, and the first thing anyone notices is that it is beautiful, which is not a detail the bestiaries enjoy including but is in every eyewitness account.

It strikes with a tail that cracks like a breaking wave, and calls tsunamis that take a whole line at once. Neither is what makes it a boss. Sylphice *mends* — wound it and the scales draw closed over the cut, unhurriedly, the way water closes over a thrown stone, and the damage of the last thirty seconds is simply no longer part of the conversation.

To kill it you must break it faster than the sea can put it back together, which is a specific and unforgiving requirement: not more total damage, but more damage in a shorter window than any single company can usually bring. Half the hunts that fail against Sylphice do so having landed more than enough blows to kill it three times over, spread across an afternoon it spent quietly undoing them.
The Ash Grove burned in the last dry wee:
The Ash Grove burned in the last dry week of a very long summer, when one strike of lightning was enough. Almost nothing in it survived. Thorneveil did, and has spent every year since deciding what that means.

He was the grove's warden, its oldest tree, and the fire went into him and never came out. He stands twice a man's height, all charred bark and splintered limbs, with blackened branches rising from his head like antlers and pale blossoms still opening on them. In the hollow of his chest, where the heartwood burned away, a flame of sickly green has never gone out. It is not fire, exactly. It is the grove, still growing, in the only form it has left.

He fights with both halves of what happened to him. The roots beneath the enemy catch and burn green, and keep burning. The boughs overhead give way and come down across whole ranks, pinning them stunned beneath the weight. And everything that stands with him grows back: the green fire at his heart runs out through the ground to every ally on the field, and their wounds close as if spring were arriving under their feet. The Ash Grove is green again, if you look closely. It is simply not the same green.
The Black Kiln is the only forge in the:
The Black Kiln is the only forge in the Emberweave that has never gone out, and Brukk is the reason, because he carries it. He was the last master of a smithing clan under the Iron Reach, and when the clan dwindled to one old smith and a cold hall, he did what no smith is supposed to do. He had the kiln taken down stone by stone and rebuilt on an iron harness across his shoulders. Its chimney still smokes above his head, and the soot is baked so deep into his skin that he has been no colour but black for forty years.

Everything about him is tempered. Blows skid off him the way a careless hammer skids off hard steel.

He fights like a smith at the anvil, and the anvil is you. The great hammer comes down, the ground for yards around jumps, and everyone on it stays down for a long ringing moment. His chain is the quenching chain from the old forge. He flings the nearest enemy far across the field with it, then casts it for the farthest and drags them in to be worked. He is not cruel. He has simply never met a thing that could not be improved by a beating.
The Briar March is a border country, fou:
The Briar March is a border country, fought over so long that the brambles have grown up through every battlefield and knitted them into one thicket: a hundred miles of thorn with the rusting armour of nine wars still hanging in it. Miregor rules it because nobody else could survive the job.

He is the size of a small house, a boar that learned to stand and wear plate, with a stag's antlers rising above his tusks, grown so twisted they look like the briar itself. His weapon is a drum of studded iron on a haft as thick as a young tree. He has never once retreated.

He is a king in the old sense, the sense that means he goes first. He stampedes through the whole enemy line to reach the farthest of them, and everything near the place he lands goes down. Then he gores, three savage heaves of the tusks that leave long wounds bleeding. But what his enemies remember is how he watches his own side. Whoever among his people is closest to falling, Miregor is standing in front of them, and part of every blow meant for them lands on him. The March has not had a good king in two hundred years. It has had a very stubborn one.
The ash barrens were farmland once. Cind:
The ash barrens were farmland once. Cindertusk are what the fire left behind when it had finished with the topsoil and moved on to the things living on it — wild furnace-beasts with hides cracked open in a lattice of living magma, each fissure breathing when the animal breathes. They are not undead and not summoned. They are simply pigs that the barrens kept.

A Cindertusk opens by gouting burning breath across whatever stands in front of it, which is less an attack than a way of finding out where everyone is. Then it rears and comes down, and the ground it lands on erupts — a blast of cinder and shock that lifts an entire front rank off their feet and fills the air with enough ash that the second charge arrives unseen.

Herds are worse than individuals by an order nobody expects, because they cook the field between them. Whole companies have been broken without a single Cindertusk closing to horn range, simply by being made to stand in air that had stopped being breathable.
The astronomers of Carrow built armillar:
The astronomers of Carrow built armillaries to model the heavens: brass rings for the orbits, a lamp at the centre for the sun, clockwork to turn it all. The finest was so exact that on the night the observatory lost Umbris, somebody noticed it was keeping better time than the stars. Then its lamp lit itself, and the whole thing rose off its stand and left through the dome.

There are dozens of them now, and nobody at Carrow will say how. A Luminant Orb is a cage of turning golden rings around a fierce knot of blue-white light, trailing a comet's tail of glow and humming the note of its own gears.

It fights like a lens. The light at its heart narrows to a single line and goes straight through the enemy rank to the farthest one standing. When threatened it flares, a burst like sunrise in a shuttered room, and whoever it faces stands blinded for a breath, along with everyone beside them. The astronomers who study the Orbs wear smoked glass. They learned that from the ones who did not.
The boar clans of the southern hills wer:
The boar clans of the southern hills were farmers once, and most still are. The Ironjaws are the ones who found that raiding paid better and never went back. You can tell them from their cousins at a distance by the cloaks, always red, and by the plate of riveted iron strapped over the snout and jaw.

The iron jaw is earned. A young raider receives it after his first successful raid, and it is riveted, not buckled, so it never comes off. Old Ironjaws eat through a gap between the plates. They consider this a matter of pride.

They fight in the loud, practical style of people who do this for a living. The axe comes round in a wide flat sweep that takes everyone in front of it at once, like a scythe through standing corn. When a fight runs long, he stamps and kicks at the ground in the beat of the clan war drum, and his swings come faster and faster until the axe is a blur. Nobody has ever heard of an Ironjaw raid being called off. They simply end.
The foundry temples of the Iron Reach ta:
The foundry temples of the Iron Reach taught that metal is purified by fire and people are no different. The acolytes wore red, kept the sacred crucible burning, and once a year poured it over the temple steps to burn away whatever the town had done wrong.

When the ore ran out and the towns emptied, the acolytes stayed, because a crucible is not permitted to go cold. They are still there, in long red robes and spiked iron masks, and whether anything remains under the masks has never been settled; they have not been seen to eat. Some left to tend a larger fire, one that walks.

They have kept the ceremony and extended it to visitors. The acolyte tips its crucible, and a slow sheet of molten flame spills across the ground where the enemy stands thickest and goes on burning there. When anyone comes to object, it draws the heat around itself like a vestment, and most of what strikes it never arrives. They are not being cruel. By their doctrine, they are purifying you.
The lamplighters of Sayle had a bad cent:
The lamplighters of Sayle had a bad century. Lamplighters were expensive, and the answer, sold to the council at a very good price, was a street lantern that walked its own route at dusk, lit itself, and walked home at dawn. They worked beautifully for eleven years. Then the workshop that built them closed, and nobody was left who knew how to stop them.

A Clockwork Lantern is an ornate cage of blackened brass around a flame that has not needed oil in a very long time, carried in quick, bird-like hops on jointed brass legs that end in talons. Most still keep to their streets. The ones that have wandered off them are not harmless.

The shutters snap open on one side and the lamp throws a single hard beam across the ground, narrow and white-hot, that scorches everything in its line. Crowded, it opens every vent at once, and the flame roars out in a ring that burns everyone close and throws them back. Somewhere in Sayle there is still a ledger with their routes in it. The lanterns would very much like it back.
The legions of the old imperial frontier:
The legions of the old imperial frontier were buried where they fell, in the forts they had been ordered to hold, with their pikes beside them and their helmets on. The orders were never countermanded. The empire was too busy falling into the Sundering to send the letter.

So the Bonepike Guards are still on duty: bronze scale over bare bone, horsehair crests gone the colour of dried blood, and the long hooked pike that was the frontier's answer to cavalry. Reach out, catch the rider, bring him down. A Guard uses it now on whoever hangs furthest back. The hook takes them under the arm and hauls them across the field to its feet, and they are held there, helpless, the whole way in.

When the line is pressed it does what it was drilled to do. It stamps and rattles and roars through a jaw with no throat behind it, and every enemy on the field can think of nothing but the skeleton. They hit it, and find it far harder to hurt than it looks. The frontier held for four hundred years. It was never the walls.
The moths of the Emberweave answer to a:
The moths of the Emberweave answer to a queen, and she has lost more of them to fire than to anything else. Most that go into the flame are simply gone. A few, on nights when the fire is large enough and full enough of grief, come out the other side.

A Mourn Moth is one of those. It is the size of a hawk, its wings ash-grey and black and printed with the pale shape of a skull, trailing ribbons of something like burnt cloth. It is drawn to funerals the way its living cousins are drawn to lamps, and the custom of shuttering the windows on the night of a wake comes from them.

In a fight it shakes itself out over the enemy, and grey dust settles over everyone below, and every arm in the cloud grows heavy, every swing a little late, the way mourners move. Then it folds its wings and drops like a stone onto whoever stands farthest away. The moth queen has never called one of them home. Nobody has asked her whether she tried.
The ossuary at Harrowmere held the bones:
The ossuary at Harrowmere held the bones of twenty generations, stacked by the monks in patterns: thighbones laid in courses like brickwork, skulls set into the walls like the heads of nails, every name lettered on the lintel above its shelf. It was the most beautiful building in the valley. By the end it was also very full.

Barrowmaw is what the ossuary became when the last monk died and nobody was left to lay the next course. It got up. It is shaped like a great cat or a wolf, depending on how it stands, made entirely of what was on those shelves and bound with the chains that once held the gates shut. Black smoke rises from its mane like grave-damp, and a single violet eye burns in the largest skull.

It hunts names. It breathes a cone of grave air over the enemy that burns the lungs and keeps burning. It hurls its whole weight of bone across the field onto the farthest one standing and scatters everyone around them. And it quickens. At the start of a fight it is slow and deliberate, as the dead are. By the end it is tearing through the ranks like something that has remembered hunger. Every name it takes goes on the lintel.
The runesmiths of the old empire did not:
The runesmiths of the old empire did not trust soldiers, so they built their own. A Runic Automaton is a hollow giant of bronze plate hung on a frame of iron bone, and every plate is cut with a word. The words are orders. The blue light burning in its chest is the word at the centre of the sentence, and it is still being obeyed.

Nobody can read the orders now, though scholars have copied whole Automatons plate by plate and argued about the grammar for decades. Its shoulder plates float a hand's breadth clear of the body, held by nothing anyone can see.

It fights by reciting. A single word leaves its hand as a bolt of blue fire and bursts where the enemy stands thickest. When it is attacked it speaks a longer word, and a ring of runes opens on the ground around it, and blows that land inside the ring lose most of their force before they reach the bronze. It is still carrying out its last order. Nobody wants to be there when it finishes.
The windriders of the high passes kept h:
The windriders of the high passes kept hawks, and the hawks kept watch, and nothing crossed the mountains unseen for three hundred years. Then a war that had no use for the passes closed them, and the riders went home, and the hawks stayed. They are still watching. They are no longer sure for whom.

A Zephyr Harrier stands like a man and is built like a hawk: grey-and-white wings, a hooked beak, talons for feet, and a scrap of teal scarf at the throat, the old colours of the pass watch. It carries a sickle, and it comes in on the wind as though the wind had been sent ahead.

It rarely closes to use the sickle. It flicks its wings twice, and two blades of cut air go spinning out at the nearest enemies. If anything reaches it, it beats down once, hard, and a ring of wind and loose feathers bursts out and sends everything close reeling. Shepherds who see a Harrier over the pass bring their flocks down early. It has never taken a sheep. It simply means someone is coming.
There are machines in the deep vaults th:
There are machines in the deep vaults that were never meant to hold a soul, and a period in the last age when several people found out what happens when you put one in anyway. Bitwraith is the residue. Not a ghost — ghosts are continuous. A Bitwraith flickers between frames, present and absent and present again, and the gap is where it does its work.

Its touch is pure static, and it rots from the inside: the wound is nowhere, the pain is everywhere, and healers report the deeply unpleasant experience of mending tissue that is fine and watching the patient continue to fail. When pressed it simply stops being where it was and resumes somewhere worse — always behind, always among the ones who were relying on not being reached.

The vaults are sealed now. This is thought to be a formality. Bitwraiths do not appear to require the machines any more, which raises a question nobody in the Emberweave has been willing to write down.
There is a drowned city off the Hollin s:
There is a drowned city off the Hollin shoals with its gates still shut, and something is still keeping them. Divers describe armoured figures standing at the posts where the city watch once stood, crusted in rose-coloured shell and spurs of coral, each with a spear of branching red coral and a shield cut from one valve of a scallop taller than a man.

Nobody knows whether the Shellguard Sentinels were the watch, or were grown to replace it, or simply moved into the armour after the watch stopped needing it. They do not seem to know either. They know the posts.

Out of the water they do not advance. They hold. The shield comes round in one heavy sweep, and everyone in front of it is knocked flat and left ringing like a struck bell. Then it is planted, the Sentinel sets its weight behind it, and blows that would crack plate slide off the nacre. Divers say the pearl in each shield glows when struck. Several have tried to pry one loose. The Sentinels kept those divers too.
There is a flower at the bottom of the S:
There is a flower at the bottom of the Sunkfen that should not grow there at all. No light reaches it. It feeds on whatever the water brings down: leaves, silt, a drowned sheep, a drowned man. The fen-cutters called it the Sunken Bloom, and for generations it was a story for keeping children away from the deep channels. Then the dykes failed, and the Bloom had more to eat than it had ever had, and it grew.

Nymira is what it became: a tall shape that grew, by accident or imitation, into something like a woman, with a crown of violet petals that open and close as she breathes and a trailing skirt of dark fronds that are not weed. They are tendrils, and they move on their own. Something glows red in her chest, and it pulses when she feeds.

She fights by feeding. Clouds of dark pollen drift from her petals and settle over the enemy, slowing them and poisoning every breath. When they come close, the tendrils lash out together at everyone within reach. And she mends constantly, like a plant turning toward the light; whatever is cut from her grows back. The fen-cutters no longer tell their children about the Bloom. The children can see it from the dyke.
This is the last chapter. It is the best:
This is the last chapter. It is the best writing in the book, and the Librarian knows it, and that has always been the problem. When he reads it aloud the ink does not step off the page so much as pour, spreading into a pool of black shot with violet light, and something heaves up out of the middle: too many shoulders, too many heads, the shape of a wolf repeated as though the writer could not settle on one.

It was not written to deal with anything in particular. It was written to be what it is. It does not hunt. It turns, every head and claw at once, in a whirl of ink that tears into everything around it, and then it turns again. Blades cut it and the ink closes behind them. It is sturdier than a page has any right to be, because he never once made a thing gentler than it was.

Then the chapter ends, and it goes home. That is the only reason he can read it at all. A town called Brisk once learned exactly how long a chapter is.
Trapjaw is an argument about greed that:
Trapjaw is an argument about greed that keeps being won. It sits in the places where a chest ought to be, and it is always the right chest — the one at the end, the one that justifies the dungeon, the one you can see from the doorway.

The bite is what people expect and it is worse than they expect: bone-crunching, disorienting, a blow that leaves an armoured man sitting down and trying to work out which way the room went. What they do not expect is that it feeds. Every hit mends the splintered lid, tightens the ruined hinge, and closes the cracks that the last party opened, so the Trapjaw that a fresh company finds is always in better repair than the one that killed the last.

There is no way to tell them from real chests. There is a way to be certain, which is to open none of them, and in four hundred years of recorded delving no party has ever adopted it.
Vharok was a warlord, and by the standar:
Vharok was a warlord, and by the standards of warlords a successful one. He took nine cities of the Iron Reach in a single campaign and lost only one fight, the last, to a fever that bred in his siege camps faster than his surgeons could bury the dead. Dying, he summoned the foundry priests of the last city he had taken and gave them one order: keep me going. They did what foundry priests know how to do. They opened his chest and built a kiln in it.

He has not been cold since. The furnace behind his ribs shows through an iron grate in his breastplate, and his armour has fused to him along cracks that glow like cooling slag. The air around him is hot enough to burn, and it does, constantly, to anyone who stands near; he does not have to aim it. Cinder Skulks follow him like crows.

He swings a spiked maul on a length of forge chain, wide enough to crush a whole rank at once. When his enemies try to scatter, rings of molten stone rise around them and lock them in place while the heat does its work. The Crucible Acolytes are still with him. They tend the kiln. Nobody has ever told them they may stop.
Voraxis is a horror of tentacle and toot:
Voraxis is a horror of tentacle and tooth that eats while it fights, and the two activities are not separable. It does not kill a company and then feed. It feeds in order to keep killing, and the fight lasts exactly as long as the food does.

It opens by pounding the earth hard enough to stagger a line, which is a herding move — a staggered formation compresses, and a compressed formation is easier to reach in one movement. Then it hurls its own bulk clear across the field to crash down among the backline, and everything it carves open feeds it, knitting its ruined flesh closed with life that was in someone else a moment earlier.

Killing it is a race against arithmetic. Every hero it wounds is subtracted from your side and added to its, and a company that fights Voraxis carefully and conservatively will lose, slowly, having done everything correctly. The ones that survive are the ones that spend everything in the first minute.
When a star falls, it does not all come:
When a star falls, it does not all come down at once. The heavy part lands, makes a crater, and gets argued about for centuries. The shards fall more slowly, and some of them, over the highest peaks where the air is thin and bitter, never finish falling at all.

Irix is built from those: a roc the size of a watchtower, feathered in blue and violet crystal that rings like struck glass when it moves and throws coloured light across the snow for miles. Nobody knows whether a great bird flew into a shower of falling stars and came out changed, or whether the shards gathered themselves into the shape of whatever owns the sky.

What happens when it comes down is not in dispute. Irix beats its wings once and its outer pinions tear loose and fall like meteors, four at a time, into whoever is nearest. When it chooses a single enemy, it drops out of the sky and takes them in its talons, and for a moment the light goes out over the whole field; when it returns, the victim is lying stunned in the snow. Every wound Irix opens goes on burning with a cold blue fire, like a star that has not finished cooling.
When the Tanglewood decides a road has c:
When the Tanglewood decides a road has come too far into it, it does not send a ranger. It sends the boars. A Vineback is a wild hog the forest has been growing on for most of its life: ivy through the bristles, moss in the folds of the hide, bramble canes rooted along the spine. Where its hooves strike, green light flickers up out of the soil, and a hoofprint in bare earth has a sprout in it by morning.

It is not clear that the boar minds. It is not clear there is much boar left to mind.

It charges the way boars charge, only more so. Head down, it crosses the whole field for whoever is furthest back, the ones with the torches and the axes, and lands among them hard enough to put them all on the ground. Then it roots, and the earth around its quarry heaves up in a tangle of living vine that locks around ankles and knees and holds everyone in it fast. The woodcutters who worked the Tanglewood roads have mostly found other work. The roads have mostly found other directions.
Where lava meets the sea it cools into b:
Where lava meets the sea it cools into black six-sided columns stacked like organ pipes, and on certain stretches of the fire coast the columns get up and walk. The Basalt Mauler is built like a great ape out of those stones: knuckle-walking, arms longer than its legs, a chest that glows faintly through the joints where the rock has never finished cooling.

The iron bands on its forearms are cooper's hoops, and every Mauler wears them. The kind theory is that someone once bound a cracking Mauler to save it, and the rest copied. The other theory is that coopers on the fire coast are rarer than they used to be.

Its fighting is simple. It raises both banded fists and brings them down, and the ground in front of it breaks outward in a wedge that throws the whole front rank off its feet. When it is hurt it hunches and lets the heat rise to the surface, and the outer stone softens, glows, and sets again harder than before. For a while after that, nothing short of a siege hammer does much.
Where lightning strikes a salt flat it f:
Where lightning strikes a salt flat it fuses the crust into glass, and the flats on the edge of the Bright Waste are strewn with it: twisted tubes and fans and wing-shapes, some the size of a person. The salt-farmers break them up and sell them. They leave alone the ones that sing.

A Saltglass Siren is one of those shapes that kept the note of the storm that made it. It is clear as shallow water, with fins like blown glass and a crest like a spiral shell, and it swims through the air with a low hum that has drawn more than one listener toward it, smiling.

It does not need them closer. It sings its note, and everything in front of it rings and freezes, stunned, the way glass goes still just before it breaks. Then it is gone, the air shimmering where it hung, and it is already behind the weakest thing on the field, striking. The people of the Waste say a mirage only shows you what you are already running toward. The Siren is why they say it.
Wintercrag is a glacier that learned to:
Wintercrag is a glacier that learned to hate, and the learning is documented — three centuries of survey markers showing an ice field advancing down a valley it had no business entering, against the prevailing thaw, in a straight line toward a town.

It breathes a nova of splintering frost that takes a front rank off its feet, then calls down a howling blizzard that creeps outward across the field and drags everything living to a standstill. Neither is the thing to be afraid of. Every so often the cold simply reaches out — no gesture, no tell, no warning — and stops a heart mid-beat, and a hero standing in reserve at the back of the formation is abruptly a statue that has not yet worked out it should fall.

The town is still there. It pays a levy every year to a company that maintains a line of fire-pits across the valley mouth, and the company's own records make clear that the pits do not stop Wintercrag. They slow it. The levy has been paid, without interruption, for two hundred and eleven years.
Witches were once weighted and thrown of:
Witches were once weighted and thrown off the harbour wall at Low Tessary, on the theory that the sea would take them and keep them. It did take them. The theory broke down on the keeping.

A Kelp Hexer comes up out of the shallows wrapped in the weed that grew over it on the bottom, long black-green ribbons that smell of the tide line. Its face has gone to something bony and fish-like under a crown of coral, and it drifts a hand's breadth above the ground, as if it has not accepted that it is out of the water. In one hand it carries a globe of seawater that holds its shape with no glass around it.

It fights the way it was killed. A bubble of brine closes over one enemy's head and holds them, choking and rooted, for exactly as long as it takes to be terrifying. Then the globe is thrown, cold and hard, and lands with the weight of a wave behind it. Low Tessary stopped throwing witches into the sea a long time ago. It was not a change of heart.
